sections.overview: Anatomical terminology is the shared, precise vocabulary that health professionals use to describe the body's parts, their locations, and how they work. This section introduces the two paired sciences that frame the entire course — **anatomy** and **physiology** — and shows you how to break unfamiliar medical words into their parts so you can decode terms you have never seen before. Almost everything else in this subject depends on the language you build here.
sections.whyItMatters: In clinical practice, vague language is dangerous. "The pain is a little above the belly button, kind of to the right" leaves room for error; "tenderness in the right upper quadrant" does not. A nurse charts, hands off patients, reads orders, and communicates with the whole care team using standardized terms. Learning this vocabulary now means that later topics — where a muscle attaches, which way a nerve signal travels, where a catheter sits — become descriptions you can actually picture rather than lists to memorize.
sections.learningObjectives:
By the end of this section you should be able to:

- Distinguish **anatomy** from **physiology** and explain how they depend on each other.
- Name the major **subdivisions of anatomy** and what each studies.
- State the **principle of complementarity** of structure and function.
- Break medical terms into **prefix, root, and suffix** to work out their meaning.
sections.keyTerms:
- **Anatomy** — the study of the structure of body parts and their relationships to one another.
- **Physiology** — the study of the function of body parts: how they work and carry out life-sustaining activities.
- **Gross (macroscopic) anatomy** — structures visible to the naked eye.
- **Microscopic anatomy** — structures too small to see without magnification (includes **cytology**, the study of cells, and **histology**, the study of tissues).
- **Complementarity of structure and function** — the principle that what a structure can do is always tied to its form.
- **Word root** — the core meaning of a term (often a body part or system).
- **Prefix** — a word part added to the front that modifies meaning (often location, number, or timing).
- **Suffix** — a word part added to the end that usually indicates a condition, procedure, or quality.
sections.collegeNotes:
**Anatomy and physiology are two views of the same body.** Anatomy asks *what a structure is and where it sits*; physiology asks *what it does and how*. You cannot fully understand one without the other. The kidney's function (filtering blood, making urine) makes sense only once you know its internal structure; and its microscopic structure looks the way it does precisely because of the job it performs.

Anatomy is usually divided by the scale at which you look. **Gross anatomy** deals with structures you can see unaided, and it can be organized in different ways: **regional anatomy** studies all structures in one body area (for example, everything in the forearm), while **systemic anatomy** studies one organ system at a time (for example, the whole cardiovascular system). **Surface anatomy** relates internal structures to visible landmarks on the skin — useful when you palpate a pulse or locate a vein. When structures are too small to see, you move into **microscopic anatomy**: **cytology** examines individual cells, and **histology** examines tissues. **Developmental anatomy** traces structural change across the lifespan, and **embryology** focuses on the changes before birth.

Physiology is likewise subdivided, most often by organ system or by focus — for example, **neurophysiology** (how nervous tissue functions), **cardiovascular physiology** (how the heart and vessels work), and **renal physiology** (kidney function). Because function ultimately arises from the behavior of cells and molecules, physiology leans heavily on basic chemistry and cell biology, which is why those topics come early in this subject.

**The principle of complementarity of structure and function** ties the two sciences together: *what a structure can do depends on its form.* Flat sheets of tightly joined cells make good barriers; a bone thickened along its lines of stress resists breaking; the huge surface area of the small intestine's lining exists because its job is absorption. Whenever a structure seems oddly shaped, ask what function that shape serves — the answer is usually the point.

### Building and decoding medical words

Medical terms look intimidating until you see that most are assembled from a small set of reusable parts. A term generally has a **root** (the core meaning), an optional **prefix** (front), and an optional **suffix** (end). A **combining vowel** — usually "o" — is often inserted to make the word pronounceable (as in *cardi-o-logy*).

Consider **pericarditis**:

- **peri-** (prefix) = around
- **card** (root) = heart
- **-itis** (suffix) = inflammation

Put together: *inflammation of the tissue around the heart.* Once you know the parts, you can decode dozens of relatives — *carditis*, *cardiology*, *cardiomegaly*, *endocarditis* — without memorizing each separately.

A handful of high-frequency word parts will carry you a long way:

| Word part | Type | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| hyper- | prefix | above, excessive | hypertension (high blood pressure) |
| hypo- | prefix | below, deficient | hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) |
| peri- | prefix | around | pericardium (sac around the heart) |
| endo- | prefix | within, inner | endocardium (inner heart lining) |
| -itis | suffix | inflammation | dermatitis (skin inflammation) |
| -ology | suffix | study of | physiology (study of function) |
| -emia | suffix | condition of the blood | anemia (deficiency of red cells) |
| -pathy | suffix | disease | neuropathy (nerve disease) |

You will meet more of these throughout the course; each section adds the ones it needs rather than front-loading a giant list.
sections.howItWorks:
Decoding a new term is a repeatable process:

1. **Split off the suffix** at the end — it usually tells you the condition, procedure, or field ("-itis," "-ectomy," "-ology").
2. **Identify the root(s)** in the middle — usually the body part or system ("card," "hepat," "nephr").
3. **Read the prefix**, if any, at the front — often location, number, or degree ("sub-," "hyper-," "poly-").
4. **Reassemble the meaning**, reading roughly end-to-front. *Hepatitis* → "-itis" (inflammation) + "hepat" (liver) = inflammation of the liver.

Practice this on real charting terms and it quickly becomes automatic.
sections.comparisons:
| Concept | Studies… | Sample question it answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Anatomy | Structure and location | *What* is the mitral valve, and *where* is it? |
| Physiology | Function and mechanism | *How* does the mitral valve keep blood moving forward? |
| Cytology | Individual cells | What organelles power a muscle cell? |
| Histology | Tissues | How is cardiac muscle tissue organized? |

Anatomy tends to be learned by observation and memory of relationships; physiology is learned by reasoning through cause and effect. Strong students consciously toggle between the two.
sections.highYield:
### High-Yield Pre-Nursing Connections

Precise terminology is the backbone of safe documentation and communication. Charting "erythema and edema of the left lower extremity" is unambiguous in a way that "red, puffy leg" is not. Order sets, lab reports, and provider notes all assume this vocabulary, so building it now pays off in every clinical course that follows. The word-part method is especially valuable on standardized exams, where you will routinely face terms you did not specifically study but can still decode.
sections.commonConfusions:
- **Anatomy vs physiology.** Structure vs function. A quick check: if the sentence describes *what something is or where it is*, that's anatomy; if it describes *what it does or how*, that's physiology.
- **Cytology vs histology.** Cytology = cells (think "cyto" = cell); histology = tissues.
- **Prefix vs suffix.** Prefix comes first and often sets location or degree; suffix comes last and often names a condition or action.
- **"Combining vowel" vs part of the root.** The "o" in *neur-o-logy* is a linker for pronunciation, not part of the root's meaning.
sections.memoryAids:
- **"Struc-ture = Anat-omy; Func-tion = Physi-ology."** Both pairs share their first sound (S/A is the exception — instead pair *Anatomy = Appearance*, *Physiology = Performance*).
- **Suffix first, prefix last, root in the middle** — decode a word from its ends inward.
- **-itis = "irritated"** (both start with "i") to remember inflammation.

*(Memory aids are learning shortcuts, not substitutes for understanding the terms themselves.)*
sections.eli10:
### ELI-10 Explains

### Simple idea
Doctors and nurses use a special word-building kit so everyone means exactly the same thing. Long scary words are really just small word-blocks snapped together.

### Analogy
Think of medical words like LEGO builds. Each word is made of a few standard bricks: a front brick (prefix), a middle brick (root), and an end brick (suffix). Once you know what each brick means, you can look at a build you've never seen and figure out what it is.

### What is actually happening
The "middle brick" is the **word root**, and it usually names a body part (like *cardi* for heart). The "front brick" is the **prefix**, which often tells you *where* or *how much* (like *peri-* for "around"). The "end brick" is the **suffix**, which often tells you *what's wrong or what you're doing* (like *-itis* for "inflammation"). Snap them together — *peri* + *cardi* + *itis* — and you get "inflammation around the heart," which is the real medical term **pericarditis**. Meanwhile, **anatomy** just means the body's *parts* (what and where), and **physiology** means how those parts *work*.

### Where the analogy stops
Unlike LEGO, you can't snap the bricks in any order — the prefix always goes first and the suffix always goes last, and sometimes a little "o" is added just to make the word easier to say. The meaning also has to make medical sense, so the kit has rules a toy set doesn't.
sections.quickReview:
- **Anatomy** = structure and location; **physiology** = function and mechanism; each explains the other.
- Anatomy subdivides by scale (gross vs microscopic — cytology for cells, histology for tissues) and by approach (regional, systemic, surface).
- **Complementarity of structure and function**: form fits job — when a structure looks unusual, ask what function that form serves.
- Decode medical terms by splitting off the **suffix**, finding the **root**, and reading the **prefix**; a few high-frequency parts unlock many terms.
